The African sharptooth catfish, a hybrid between Clarias gariepinus and Heterobranchus longifilis, exhibits rapid early development that is strongly modulated by thermal conditions. Under controlled laboratory conditions, the age at which the fertilised eggs undergo eclosion was found to be tightly linked to incubation temperature. At a constant water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], hatching occurred after approximately 1.25 days [ab = approximately 1.25 days], whereas at a warmer regime of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], the chorion rupture was observed much sooner, at just 0.58 days [ab = 0.58 days]. This inverse relationship between temperature and hatching duration is consistent with the accelerated embryonic metabolic rates typical of tropical siluriforms and reflects the species' adaptation to warm, fluctuating floodplain environments where rapid hatching can reduce egg predation risk. The prolarvae that emerge at eclosion are minute, with individual wet weight at birth calculated from the average egg diameter of 1.5 mm to be approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams]. This tiny initial mass underscores the substantial parental investment required to produce a large number of relatively small, yolk-dependent larvae that must quickly transition to exogenous feeding.

Juvenile and adult growth trajectories of this hybrid are equally noteworthy, with individuals capable of attaining considerable size. The ultimate total length reported for this species reaches 170 cm [Li = 170 cm], placing it among the larger catfishes in African freshwater systems. Achieving such a length is accompanied by a correspondingly large ultimate wet weight, which has been documented to reach as high as 60,000 grams [Wwi = 60,000 grams] in the most robust adults. This substantial body size is thought to confer advantages in both intraspecific competition and predator avoidance, though it also imposes higher absolute metabolic demands. The reproductive biology of the hybrid is first triggered upon reaching a certain body size threshold; field data indicate that wet weight at puberty is approximately 1,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,000 grams], or a little over a kilogram. Only individuals exceeding this mass typically exhibit gonadal recrudescence and participate in the spawning aggregations that occur during the rainy season, suggesting that a critical body condition must be met before energetic investment in reproduction becomes viable.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of the hybrid has been assessed in mature females. At a stable water temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C], the gonadosomatic index was measured at 0.7% [GSI = 0.7%]. Fecundity per reproductive event has been quantified in field studies, with gravid females producing approximately 50,000 eggs per spawning. Furthermore, examination of ovarian development across the annual cycle indicates that individual females may complete one spawning event per year, presumably timed to coincide with seasonal flood pulses that provide optimal nursery habitat for the pelagic larvae.

Longevity in this species is surprisingly extended relative to many other tropical catfishes, a trait that may be linked to its large body size and relatively slow growth rate after maturity. Using mark-recapture data and validated by otolith annuli counts, the maximum recorded life span under natural conditions in the wild has been estimated at 15 years [am = 15 years] at an average water temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. This extended life span, combined with the relatively low gonadal investment and repeat spawning, fits a "bet-hedging" life-history strategy common among large-bodied, long-lived teleosts inhabiting unpredictable environments. The capacity to survive and reproduce over many years likely cushions the population against recruitment failures in years when flood conditions are suboptimal for larval survival. In contrast to the short-lived, semelparous death observed in some smaller clariids, this hybrid appears to exhibit senescence gradually, with older individuals maintaining reproductive viability well into their second decade of life.

Physiologically, the early life stages of this hybrid catfish demonstrate how thermal conditions not only dictate hatching time but also influence the timing of key developmental milestones. The lecithotrophic phase, during which the yolk-sac larvae rely entirely on endogenous reserves, is brief and highly temperature-dependent. After the onset of exogenous feeding, the free-swimming larvae enter a period of rapid growth. Comparisons with wild populations suggest that the life span commonly recorded in stable, warm-water impoundments may be reduced under more thermally variable riverine conditions. Body composition analyses reveal that the neonates, weighing just 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams] at hatching, must increase their mass by over seven orders of magnitude to approach the ultimate wet weight of 60,000 grams [Wwi = 60,000 grams] characteristic of large adults. This phenomenal growth trajectory places extreme demands on foraging efficiency and habitat quality during the juvenile fingerling stage. Understanding the interplay between temperature, growth, and reproduction is therefore critical for managing the species in both aquaculture settings and natural floodplain ecosystems.
